layers.description: Brand-themed React primitives and product components in packages/ui (with CSS modules, formatting helpers and tests), plus the Vite ui-preview app that showcases them across themes.

layers.name: Storefront Pages and Components
layers.description: Next.js App Router pages, layouts, cart state and feature components of the mobile-first jewellery storefront, with their CSS modules and tests, plus the Playwright browser and accessibility tests in apps/web/e2e.

layers.name: Storefront Services and Runtime
layers.description: Server-side side of the web app: catalog and policy data access, SEO, robots and sitemap, health and readiness routes, database pool, security headers, startup validation and Next.js config.

layers.name: Domain Logic and Persistence
layers.description: Pricing, silver composition and stock reservation rules in packages/domain, and the Drizzle schema, SQL migrations, migration runner and reference-data seed in packages/db.

layers.name: Design Tokens and Theming
layers.description: Base, component and per-theme token JSON in packages/design-tokens with the scripts that build, validate and scaffold themes.

layers.name: Configuration and Tooling
layers.description: Validated runtime configuration in packages/config, workspace manifests, TypeScript, Vitest and lint settings, environment template and repository check and smoke scripts.

layers.name: Infrastructure and CI/CD
layers.description: Docker image and Compose services for local runs, and GitHub Actions workflows for CI, design-token checks and staging and production deployment.

layers.name: Documentation
layers.description: Product and design briefs, READMEs, ADRs, setup and runbook guides, brand copy, audits, phase plans and specs.

tour.title: What Argiva Is
tour.description: Start with the README: this is the website and online store for ARGIVA Silvers, a silver jewellery business. It lists the folders under apps/ and packages/, how to run the site, and what is not built yet (checkout, payments and the admin dashboard). The product brief explains who the site is for and what the brand promises, which is the reason behind many choices you will see later.

tour.title: How The Repo Fits
tour.description: The code lives in one repository with several apps and shared packages, often called a monorepo. The workspace file says which folders are packages, the root package.json holds the everyday build and test commands, and the Turborepo file says in what order to run them. The tech stack decision record explains why the team chose to build a custom TypeScript application.
tour.languageLesson: A pnpm workspace lets one package import another by name, such as @argiva/ui, without publishing it anywhere.

tour.title: The Home Page
tour.description: This is the main entry point of the storefront, the page a visitor sees first. It loads the active categories and then puts together a hero banner and three smaller sections: the collection grid, the family heritage story and the brand promise. Read it as a table of contents: each part it imports does one visible job.
tour.languageLesson: In the Next.js App Router, the folder path under app/ becomes the web address, and a page.tsx file is what that address shows. Components run on the server unless the file opts in to running in the browser.

tour.title: The Shared Page Frame
tour.description: The root layout wraps every page, including the home page you just read. It reads the app settings, picks the theme, adds search engine information, and places the header, cart drawer and footer around the page content. It also sets up the theme and cart providers, which share data with any component below them.
tour.languageLesson: A React context provider makes a value, such as the cart or the theme, available to all child components without passing it down by hand.

tour.title: Reusable Building Blocks
tour.description: The pages are built from shared components in packages/ui, and the index file is the public list of what that package offers. The Hero and ProductCard are good first examples, and the theme provider tells components which visual theme is active. The preview app shows these components in each theme, so you can see them without the store.
tour.languageLesson: CSS modules (files ending .module.css) keep class names local to one component, so styles do not clash.

tour.title: Themes And Design Tokens
tour.description: Colours, spacing and fonts are not typed directly into components; they are stored as named values called design tokens. The default quiet-luxury theme file is one set of those values, the build script turns tokens into CSS and a list of themes, and the validate script blocks bad values such as poor colour contrast. DESIGN.md describes how the default theme should look and feel.
tour.languageLesson: A token can point to another token, so a component asks for a meaning (for example a surface colour) and each theme decides the actual value.

tour.title: Catalog Data For Pages
tour.description: The catalog file is the most depended-on file in the project, so it is worth reading carefully. The home, collection, product and search pages go through it to get categories, products, variants and approved silver rates, and it works out prices with the pricing rules you will meet shortly. Pages therefore do not need to write their own database queries.
tour.languageLesson: The tests replace the database with hand-built stand-ins (mocks), so the query logic can be checked without a running Postgres.

tour.title: Browsing And Product Pages
tour.description: With the data layer in mind, follow a shopper from a collection to a single product. The bracketed [slug] folders are one page template that serves many addresses, the collection results filter products in the browser, and the product page hands the interactive part to a purchase panel where the shopper picks a variant. A variant is one sellable version of a product, with its own purity, weight, finish and price.
tour.languageLesson: A 'client component' runs in the browser and can react to clicks; keeping these small lets most of the page be rendered on the server.

tour.title: The Shopping Cart
tour.description: Adding a variant on the product page puts it into the cart. The cart context keeps the items in the browser's local storage and offers actions and totals, while the slide-over drawer and the cart page display them. There is no server-side order yet, because checkout is a later phase.
tour.languageLesson: useSyncExternalStore is a React hook for reading data that lives outside React, such as local storage, and re-drawing when it changes.

tour.title: Pricing And Honesty Rules
tour.description: The domain package holds the business rules as plain functions that do not depend on the website or the database. Pricing works in whole paise, using either a fixed price or the silver rate, and can freeze a snapshot of an order's price. The composition rules ensure unverified silver purity is never presented as confirmed, and the reservation rules hold stock for a limited time.
tour.languageLesson: Storing money as integers (paise) avoids the small rounding errors that decimal numbers cause.

tour.title: Database And Seed Data
tour.description: The schema file describes the tables behind the catalog data you saw earlier: categories, products, variants, silver rates, orders and more. The SQL migrations create those tables in Postgres, the package index provides the database connection, the migration runner applies those migrations, and the seed file adds reference data: the categories and draft policy pages, with no sample products. Policy pages are stored here too, added by the second migration.
tour.languageLesson: Drizzle defines tables in TypeScript and generates SQL migration files from them; migrations are applied in order and are not run automatically here.

tour.title: Settings And Safe Startup
tour.description: Settings such as the site address, database address and theme come from environment variables, and only the config package reads them. The schema checks each value, the instrumentation check stops the server with a readable message if something is wrong, and the readiness route reports whether the database answers. The .env.example file is the template for your local settings.
tour.languageLesson: Zod validates data while the program runs and also produces the matching TypeScript type from the same definition.

tour.title: Build, Test And Deploy
tour.description: The Dockerfile packages the web app into a container image in two stages, one to build and one to run. Docker Compose starts that app with a local database. The CI workflow builds, lints, type-checks, unit tests, smoke tests and runs real-browser tests, and the staging and production workflows use a shared deploy workflow to create database tables, load reference data and release to Google Cloud Run.
tour.languageLesson: A multi-stage Docker build keeps build tools out of the final image. In GitHub Actions, a reusable workflow lets two pipelines share the same deploy steps.

tour.title: Where To Go Next
tour.description: The docs index links to the rest of the written material. Use the setup guide for one-time accounts and services, the runbook for day-to-day operations, and the 25 November project audit to learn what is broken or missing in Phases 1 to 4 as of that date. The roadmap shows the project phases still to come.
